title: Argali horns share a spiral angle but differ in their shearing (helical) component

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Argali horns share a spiral angle but differ in their shearing (helical) component

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Among closely allied wild sheep (Argali) the constant angle of the horn's logarithmic spiral is nearly the same, and the species differ chiefly in the helical shearing component.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XIII: The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: In all of these the constant angle of the logarithmic spiral is very much the same, but the shearing component differs greatly.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XIII, “The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion”; topic “Helical component of horns”. Scope: Asiatic wild sheep (Ovis ammon, O. poli, O. hodgsoni)

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch13-05: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.74

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: This is a clear comparison of two geometric parameters using standard 3D methods. Existing museum media likely suffice for a focused test, although population-level coverage may be limited.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Decompose 3D horn centerlines from Ovis ammon, O. poli and O. hodgsoni into planar logarithmic angle and out-of-plane helical components. Similar estimated spiral angles but significantly different torsion support the claim; substantial angle differences or similar torsion refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Public 3D sample sizes for rare wild sheep may be small.

Taxonomic synonymy and specimen age require curation.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Separating a shared spiral angle from a differing shear is a well-posed 3D measurement and would cleanly support or reject the comparison among these sheep. Public scans and photographs of the three species are sparse and often show the skull without a full horn, so the test is limited to whatever intact specimens can be assembled. The decision criterion itself is strong; the sample is the obstacle.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Decompose each argali horn into a logarithmic angle in the generating plane and a helical pitch, then compare Ovis ammon, O. poli, and O. hodgsoni. The claim is supported if the logarithmic angles agree within measurement error while pitch differs; a species difference in the logarithmic angle as large as the difference in pitch would refute the stated partition.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Complete sheaths of all three named argali are scarce in open 3D repositories.

Single photographs confound the in-plane angle with the helical component.
